source: Wyrich (2023) Source Code Comprehension: A Contemporary Definition and Conceptual Model (history section on Brooks)
finding: Brooks (1978, 1983) is the root of the top-down model. Understanding is successive refinement of hypotheses. The first hypothesis forms as soon as the developer gets any information. Beacons in the code (comments, names) confirm or refute hypotheses. Brooks first used the word beacon in 1983.
numbers: No experiment numbers in this review. Brooks essay 1978, elaboration 1983.
quote: successive refinement of hypotheses about the program's operation
limits: Secondary account of Brooks. The Brooks papers themselves were not opened. Wyrich also notes that different ways of measuring comprehension mostly do not correlate with each other, so results across studies are hard to compare.
agent_relevance: S1/S2: reading code as hypothesis, check against beacons, refine. Fits an operator that states a guess about what a function does and tests it against names and comments.

source: Wyrich (2023) (Pennington, Letovsky, Littman et al. as told by the review)
finding: Pennington (1987) showed that procedural (control-flow) units, not functional units, form the first mental representation of experts: the program model. A situation model (data flow plus goal hierarchy) is built after it. Letovsky (1987) models the understander as knowledge base + evolving mental model + assimilation process, an opportunistic processor. Littman et al. split programmers into systematic and as-needed readers, and into static versus causal knowledge. Systematic readers did better at the modification task.
numbers: Pennington: two studies, in both control flow and procedures were understood before functions. Weak model = static knowledge only; strong model = static plus causal.
quote: is best viewed as an opportunistic processor
limits: Second-hand. The Pennington, Letovsky and Littman originals were not opened (paywalled). Pennington study 1 used small code snippets.
agent_relevance: Two reading phases: first trace what the code does step by step, then ask what it is for. Supports an order of operators in S1: structure first, purpose second.

source: Wyrich (2023) (Gilmore's model of debugging as told by the review)
finding: Gilmore (1991) argues that debugging does not use a finished comprehension model built in an earlier step. Comprehension runs inside the debugging loop, and the key event is a mismatch between the programmer's expectation and the code. Bugs deeper in the program structure were found more easily, which a compare-with-a-finished-model view does not predict.
numbers: No sample sizes given in the review.
quote: Both groups of programmers were more likely to find the deeper bugs, suggesting that they were being detected during an ongoing comprehension process
limits: Quote is Gilmore as cited by Wyrich. Gilmore 1991 was not opened. Evidence base is small debugging studies.
agent_relevance: Reading and debugging are one loop: keep an explicit expected-behaviour statement and treat a mismatch with the code or output as the trigger to look deeper.

source: Wyrich (2023) (Koenemann and Robertson; von Mayrhauser and Vans metamodel as told by the review)
finding: Review states Koenemann and Robertson (1991) found as-needed reading driven by the developer's goal, mostly top-down, with bottom-up used only when hypotheses are missing or fail and locally for directly relevant code. The 1995 integrated metamodel joins Soloway-Ehrlich top-down, Pennington program and situation models, and a knowledge base, and any component can be activated at any time.
numbers: Metamodel has 4 components: top-down model, program model, situation model, knowledge base.
quote: in cases of missing or failing hypotheses and locally for directly relevant code units
limits: A 2023 preprint under review. It also says no accepted definition of code comprehension exists.
agent_relevance: The scaffold should allow switching between modes, not fix one order.

source: Fekete and Porkolab (2020) A comprehensive review on software comprehension models
finding: Review of comprehension models. Static elements: beacons, chunks, hypotheses (why, how, what), plans, rules of discourse, text-structure knowledge. Dynamic: chunking and cross-referencing. Top-down: Brooks, Soloway-Adelson-Ehrlich. Bottom-up: Shneiderman-Mayer, Pennington. Combined: Letovsky, von Mayrhauser integrated metamodel. Concludes developers do not follow one rigid model and work opportunistically.
numbers: Cites Corbi 1989 (IBM): over 50% of working hours go to static analysis of code; Microsoft 2007 survey: 95% said comprehension matters, 65% do it at least daily.
limits: Survey, no new data. Editor-feature classification is the authors' own judgement.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary (beacon, chunk, hypothesis, plan) for the scaffold's read-code operators.

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems (IWPC)
finding: 75 participants of mixed skill debugged a Stata program for 20 minutes after a 10-minute tutorial. Four planted bugs. Hierarchical clustering of comprehension-behaviour measures gave three strategies: depth-first (cluster 1), inactive (cluster 2), breadth-first with most programming experience (cluster 3). No strategy was clearly best. Bug-specific domain knowledge predicted success best.
numbers: N=75 of 86 recruited (11 dropped for poor English). Clusters of 20, 40, 15. Mean bugs fixed (0-4): 1.00, 1.65, 2.00; cluster 1 lower than 2 and 3 (p<.05). Cluster vs major p<.01; programming experience differed by cluster (p<.01). Inverted-axes bug fixed by 16 of 75 (21.3%), the least often.
limits: Exploratory, not a controlled test. Cluster solution chosen by judgement (3 of 2-7 tried). Unfamiliar environment (Stata) and a statistics domain, not professional code. Cluster sizes unequal.
agent_relevance: In a new tool or codebase the reading strategy mattered less than domain knowledge. The agent should pull in domain facts for the bug at hand before reading broadly.

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) related-work predictions of von Mayrhauser-Vans and Gilmore
finding: Ko and Uttl state the theory predictions for an unfamiliar system. Von Mayrhauser and Vans: control and data flow are built bottom-up, with more use of documentation and domain knowledge. Gilmore: a reconstructive process where perceived design decisions are compared with actual behaviour, so unfamiliarity is a bottleneck but should not change strategy. Their data show strategy did vary with experience, and strategy did not predict success the way earlier work on familiar systems did.
numbers: Three clusters, 75 participants. The most experienced (cluster 3) used a breadth-first pattern.
limits: The interpretation is the authors' on one small exploratory study.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition: findings from reading familiar code in a familiar language may not hold when the agent faces an unfamiliar library.

source: Koenemann and Robertson (1991) Expert problem solving strategies for program comprehension (CHI '91)
finding: 12 experienced Pascal programmers modified a 636-line formatter program (main plus 39 procedures) in one of 4 tasks. Information was served one piece at a time on request. They did not read systematically. They studied only code relevant to the task, read an overview first, then looked for directly relevant code (a focused top-down process), and used bottom-up reading only for directly relevant code or when hypotheses failed.
numbers: N=12, 4 to 15 years programming (mean 7.6), Pascal 4+ years. 15 to 44 min per task. Subjects visited on average about one fifth of the procedures and under one third of the lines; none studied more than about half. On average 24% of procedures (21.3% of lines) were never even encountered. Chart use fell linearly over time F(1,11)=36.05, p<.001; code use rose linearly, p<.001.
quote: a pragmatic as-needed rather than a systematic strategy
limits: Qualifies Littman et al. (small programs, where systematic reading helped); authors credit the larger program. Information shown by request is a lab artifact, though all subjects said it felt normal. 12 people over 4 tasks.
agent_relevance: For big repos the agent cannot read everything. As-needed, goal-driven reading is what experts do. The risk is partial models, so add a coverage check for the parts that matter.

source: Koenemann and Robertson (1991) relevance classes and names
finding: Subjects judged code as directly relevant, intermediate or strategic. Relevance was hypothesised from procedure names and domain knowledge. Subjects decoded abbreviated names (getcmd for getcommand) very well. Different tasks led to different code being studied.
numbers: Example: the underline procedure was studied by all subjects with bold or underline tasks but by none of the others; the footer/header procedure put1 by 5 of 6 subjects whose tasks needed it.
limits: One program, one language, tiny N. Names were decodable, which may not hold for obfuscated code.
agent_relevance: Names are beacons. The agent should use identifiers to guess relevance, and verify when names could mislead.

source: von Mayrhauser and Vans (1997) Program understanding behavior during debugging of large scale software
finding: Field observation of 4 professional maintainers debugging code of at least 40,000 lines in think-aloud sessions. They switched between program, situation and top-down models. Chunking and storing information, using knowledge and generating hypotheses were top actions at all levels. Domain knowledge drove top-down work. A programmer with language skill but no domain knowledge stayed at lower levels of abstraction.
numbers: N=4, sessions about 2 hours. Chunk-and-store counts: program model 115, situation model 107. Reading code in sequence: 102. Hypothesis generation: 76 top-down, 64 situation, 65 program. Domain knowledge was 23% of top-down actions (count 107). Three domain experts made 94% of top-down references. The language expert with no domain experience made 13% of his references at domain level.
limits: Authors call the conclusions working hypotheses: sample too small. Observational; each subject had a different task, language and software, so expertise is confounded with task.
agent_relevance: Domain knowledge lets a reader jump from code to purpose. Without it the reader stays on the code. The scaffold should supply domain context early.

source: Vans, von Mayrhauser and Somlo (1999) Program understanding behavior during corrective maintenance of large-scale software (IJHCS 51)
finding: Journal version of the same four-subject field study. Programmers work at code, algorithm and domain levels about equally and switch often. Their main questions are what the software does and how, not why it was built so. Information is cross-referenced across many sources, which tools make hard. Hypotheses structure the work.
numbers: N=4 subjects, software of 40,000+ lines, about 2-hour sessions. Subject C1 (language expert, domain novice) had 14% of model references in the domain model.
quote: Programmers work at all levels of abstraction about equally
limits: Same limits as the conference version: 4 subjects, expertise crossed with person and task.
agent_relevance: A single fixed order (bottom-up only or top-down only) is a poor default.

source: Singer and Lethbridge (WESS 1998) Just-in-time comprehension vs. the full-coverage strategy
finding: A two-year longitudinal case of one software engineer in a telecom company. For routine maintenance and bug fixes he comprehended only the code needed (just-in-time) and the partial model faded. For a new feature he went for full coverage and wrote analysis documents. Strategy depended on the goal, not the person. They renamed Littman's as-needed and systematic strategies.
numbers: N=1 engineer, meetings every 1 to 6 weeks over about 2 years, plus 30 minutes of observation per meeting.
quote: What determines usage is not 'SE-type,' but rather SE goal
limits: A one-person position paper. Not statistical.
agent_relevance: Choose strategy by task: narrow fix gets as-needed reading, new feature or refactor gets broad coverage. Make that a code-checked branch on task type.

source: Burkhardt, Detienne and Wiedenbeck (2002) Object-oriented program comprehension: effect of expertise, task and phase (Empirical Software Engineering)
finding: A test of Pennington's program-model versus situation-model paradigm on object-oriented code. Experts beat novices overall. Situation-model questions were answered better than program-model questions. In documentation, experts and novices differed on the situation model but not the program model. For novices doing reuse, the situation model grew over time while the program model did not. A task that demands it makes novices build a situation model.
numbers: N=51 (30 experts, 21 novices), 4-hour sessions, 35 min study then 90 min task. Correctness: expert 67.8 vs novice 63.9, F(1,46)=6.84, p<.012; situation 73.1 vs program 59.4, F(1,46)=99.3, p<.0001; phase 1 63.9 to phase 2 68.5, F(1,46)=15.5; documentation 67.9 vs reuse 64.7, F(1,46)=4.23, p<.046. Four-way interaction of expertise, phase, task and model type.
quote: novices do not spontaneously construct a strong situation model but are able to do so if the task demands it
limits: Program-model-first was not tested directly: the authors say question difficulty cannot be calibrated, so the two models are not comparable. OO code (C++), not Pennington's procedural code. An extension, not a clean replication.
agent_relevance: A boundary on the bottom-up claim: the task shapes the representation. Give the agent a purpose-driven task (will I reuse this?) to push it toward a goal-level model, not only line tracing.

source: Detienne (survey) What model(s) for program understanding? (describes Pennington 1987a)
finding: Describes Pennington's test: experts read short programs, answered control-flow questions better than function questions, but after a modification task answered function questions better. Read as a program model (textbase) first, then a situation model once a task demands it. Later object-oriented models are not strictly bottom-up.
numbers: No new numbers. Direction of the Pennington 1987a result only.
limits: Secondary. Pennington's own numbers were not opened. A DTIC report page found by search says 80 programmers were tested in her first study; I did not open it.
agent_relevance: Fits two-stage reading: trace first, then derive purpose once the task is set.

source: Detienne (survey) purpose of reading changes the representation (Mills et al. 1995, as cited)
finding: The survey reports that readers with a knowledge-acquisition goal remembered more situational information than readers with other goals (Mills et al. 1995). So the reading goal shapes what is stored.
numbers: No numbers given in the survey for this point.
limits: Second-hand only. Mills et al. not opened.
agent_relevance: State the reading goal in the prompt slot before reading code.

source: Li et al. (2024) Do Machines and Humans Focus on Similar Code? (ICPC 2024)
finding: Compared eye-tracking of 27 programmers summarising Java methods with SHAP attributions of six models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, GPT-few-shot, StarCoder, Code Llama, NCS). Found no statistically significant relation between model focus and human focus. Alignment did not predict summary quality. Few-shot prompting to make summaries human-like did not raise alignment. Models leaned on comments, return values and literals, and less on method calls.
numbers: 27 programmers, 68 Java methods. At most 22% of methods gave a significant Spearman rho between a human-LLM pair, against 85% between two models. Where significant, rho was near +0.5 or -0.5.
quote: We find no evidence that feature attribution in language models is correlated with programmers' visual focus
limits: SHAP attributions are a proxy for model focus and eye fixations a proxy for human focus. Summarisation only, Java only.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the model reads code the way people do. Human reading studies suggest what to check, not how the model attends.

source: Kou et al. (2024) Do LLMs Pay Similar Attention Like Human Programmers When Generating Code? (FSE 2024)
finding: Built a dataset of programmer attention on 1,138 HumanEval and MBPP task descriptions. Six LLMs including GPT-4 showed consistent misalignment with programmers across attention methods. Five attention patterns explain 27% of 211 wrong programs analysed. Perturbation-based attention was most often preferred by programmers.
numbers: 1,138 tasks, 6 LLMs, 12 attention methods, 211 incorrect snippets (CodeGen-2.7B and GPT-4), 27% explained by 5 patterns. Labeler agreement Cohen kappa 0.64 to 0.73.
limits: Human attention here is words labelled important by two experienced programmers, not eye tracking, and on the task description rather than code reading. Generation, not comprehension.
agent_relevance: Errors tied to ignored words in the task. Supports restating the problem and checking each requirement before writing code.

source: Paltenghi, Pandita, Henley and Ziegler (2022/2024) Follow-up Attention: developer and neural model code exploration
finding: Compared attention of CodeGen, InCoder and GPT-J with developers' eye movements while answering sensemaking questions about code. A new 'follow-up attention' measure gave the highest agreement with developers. It predicts the next line a developer looks at with 47% accuracy, above a 42.3% baseline built from other developers' session histories. CodeGen, the largest model, correlated best.
numbers: 25 developers, 92 valid sessions, 45 unique tasks. Next-line accuracy 47% vs 42.3% baseline.
limits: Margin over baseline is about 5 points. Small snippets, three open models of 2022. Disagrees with the misalignment found by Li and Kou; the attention measure and task differ.
agent_relevance: Mixed evidence on human-likeness. Not strong enough to base a design on.

source: Hooda et al. (2024) Do Large Code Models Understand Programming Concepts? Counterfactual Analysis for Code Predicates (ICML 2024)
finding: Tested ten code models on mutations that should not change correctness: rename variables, flip if-else with negated condition, break a def-use chain, swap independent statements. Models lost accuracy on renames, if-else flips and def-use breaks, so they track data flow and control flow poorly. Swapping independent statements hurt least.
numbers: 10 models (Llama 2, Code Llama, PaLM 2, GPT-4-1106, StarCoder) on HumanEval, MBPP, CodeContests. Average mutation effect on unit-test correctness as high as 34%. Larger and code-trained models did better on variable renames.
limits: Models from 2023; GPT-4-1106 was the newest. Python only. The per-model table columns were hard to read from text extraction, so only the paper's stated summary is recorded.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the model to follow data flow through names alone. Use code to run or trace values.

source: Beyond Accuracy: Characterizing Code Comprehension Capabilities in (Large) Language Models (2026)
finding: Asks whether LLM code success follows human complexity measures (lexical size, control-flow complexity, AST structure). A human-metric classifier predicted model success only weakly, while a feature-free shadow model predicted it much better, so model failures follow non-human regularities.
numbers: AUROC 0.63 from human metrics vs 0.86 from the shadow model. Dataset of 799,365 (program, input, output) triples; 12,563 evaluation pairs. On SWE-bench Verified two top open systems solved 234 and 230 tasks with only 175 shared (59 and 55 unique).
limits: Preprint, output-prediction style task. AUROC 0.63 is above chance, so human metrics are weakly related, not unrelated.
agent_relevance: Human notions of difficulty (nesting, size) are weak predictors of where the agent fails. Check by running, not by guess.

source: Richards and Wessel (2024) What You Need is What You Get: Theory of Mind for an LLM-Based Code Understanding Assistant
finding: Within-subject study of an LLM assistant that infers the user's mental state (ToMMY) against a plain assistant. No overall effect on quiz scores. But users who phrased questions as hypotheses did worse with ToMMY, and others did better.
numbers: N=14 novices, 2 observations each (28). Hypothesis phrasing: 6 of 14. Without hypotheses (16 obs): ToMMY coefficient +0.34, p<.01. With hypotheses (12 obs): -0.28, p=.07. Programming experience raised quiz score; LLM familiarity lowered it (p=.02).
limits: Tiny sample. The hypothesis split was made after seeing the data. Linking it to Brooks is my reading; the paper cites Brooks only in its references.
agent_relevance: Personalised explanations may hurt people who already test their own hypotheses. A weak, preliminary signal.

source: Lehmen, Wyrich, Maurer, Peitek and Apel (2026) Predicting Program Comprehension with Foundation Models of Human Cognition
finding: Tested Centaur (a model fine-tuned on 160 psychology experiments) against its base Llama on nine published program-comprehension studies. Centaur predicted human answers better and relied less on earlier trials, more on task information. Cites bottom-up and top-down theories as background.
numbers: 9 studies. Mean negative log-likelihood Centaur 1.63 vs Llama 1.85 (p<.001, effect size 0.172). Centaur better in 7 of 9 studies: 2 negligible, 4 small, 1 medium effect.
limits: Predicts human answers to comprehension tasks, not code reading itself. Small effect sizes. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A model of human responses can be partly learned, but the gain is small. Not a basis for the scaffold.

source: Qiao, Shihab and Hundhausen (2025) Systematic Literature Review of GenAI Assistants for Code Comprehension
finding: Review of 31 studies from 2022 to 2024 on GenAI for code comprehension. States the standard view: novices read bottom-up, experts top-down using beacons. Most evidence is from lab studies of perceptions; AI explanations are often inaccurate or unclear and novices write poor prompts.
numbers: 31 papers (2022-2024). 25 of 31 lab studies. 26 collected subjective perceptions.
limits: Education-focused, mostly perceptions rather than accuracy. It does not test the classic models against model behaviour.
agent_relevance: Shows the gap: nobody has yet measured whether an LLM follows bottom-up or as-needed reading.

source: CoCoNUT: Structural Code Understanding does not fall out of a tree (ICSE LLM4Code 2025), as seen in a search result
finding: Search snippet says the best model (Gemini) fully and correctly traced only 47% of HumanEval tasks when asked for control-flow execution traces.
numbers: 47% full correct traces, best model.
limits: Only a search snippet seen. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Control-flow tracing by a model is unreliable, so execute code to get traces.

source: Vans, von Mayrhauser and Somlo (1999) background on systematic versus opportunistic strategy
finding: The paper restates Littman, Pinto, Letovsky and Soloway (1986): a systematic approach studies code completely in order and gave better modifications; an opportunistic (as-needed) approach is incomplete and makes modifications error prone. The authors add that the systematic strategy is unrealistic for large programs. Observed subjects still read code in sequence often, which they take as a systematic element.
numbers: Reading code in sequence was a top-three action at program level (count 102 in the 1997 version). 4 subjects.
limits: Littman's own numbers are not given in this paper. The claim that opportunistic reading is error prone is second-hand.
agent_relevance: Gives the trade-off the scaffold must manage: as-needed reading is cheap but leaves gaps, so pair it with a check of the assumptions it left unverified.
